title: Kepler Lab: orbital mechanics sandbox
prompt:
Build 'Kepler Lab', an orbital-mechanics sandbox in three.js for an astronomy class. Unlike a toy orrery, every position must follow Kepler's laws, because students will check the numbers.

Bodies (semi-major axis a in AU, eccentricity e, longitude of perihelion ϖ in degrees):
- Mercury: 0.387, 0.206, 77
- Venus: 0.723, 0.007, 131
- Earth: 1.000, 0.017, 103
- Mars: 1.524, 0.093, 336
- Jupiter: 5.203, 0.049, 14
- Comet Vela: 3.1, 0.72, 200

Physics, with time t in days and every body at perihelion at day 0:
- Period P = 365.25 × a^1.5 days.
- Mean anomaly M = 2π·t/P. Solve Kepler's equation E − e·sin E = M with Newton's method (to 1e-8). True anomaly ν = 2·atan2(√(1+e)·sin(E/2), √(1−e)·cos(E/2)), reported in 0–360°. Distance r = a·(1 − e·cos E). Speed from the vis-viva equation: v = 29.78 × √(2/r − 1/a) km/s.
- All orbits lie in one plane with the Sun at one focus; perihelion points in direction ϖ, measured counter-clockwise from +X seen from above, and every body moves counter-clockwise.

Scene: 1 AU = 10 scene units. A glowing Sun; planets as lit spheres with exaggerated sizes (Jupiter the largest); Comet Vela as a small bright nucleus with a tail that always points directly away from the Sun; every orbit drawn as a thin ellipse; a starfield backdrop.

HUD:
- 'Kepler Lab' at the top-left with a 'Day 0.0' readout (one decimal).
- A bottom time bar: a Play/Pause button whose label switches, speed buttons '1×', '10×' and '100×' (simulated days per real second; 10× and playing on load), a 'Day' scrubber from 0 to 4000 that pauses playback while dragged, and a 'Jump to day' number input with a 'Go' button that jumps to that day and pauses.
- Clicking a body (use a generous hit area) selects it: a highlight ring appears and a panel on the right shows its name, a, e, the period as 'Period 123.4 d', r in AU with 3 decimals, ν in degrees with 1 decimal and v in km/s with 2 decimals. The values update live while time runs. Clicking empty space or pressing Escape deselects. A 'Follow' checkbox in the panel keeps the camera centred on the selected body.
- Dragging orbits the camera and the wheel zooms.

The initial camera looks down on the orbital plane at an angle and fits Jupiter's and the comet's orbits entirely inside the 1280x720 frame.
interaction_hints: Take two screenshots 1500 ms apart and compare the Day readout (about +15 at 10×); click 100× and repeat; click Pause and confirm nothing moves. To check values: type into the Jump to day input (type with its selector and the value), click Go (time pauses), then click the body. Bodies are small: find them in a screenshot (Mars is the 4th planet from the Sun, the comet is on the elongated ellipse) and scroll to zoom in if needed; the Follow checkbox helps keep a body in view. Expected (last digit ±1): day 500 Mars Period 687.2 d, r 1.556, ν 251.6, v 23.61; day 60 Comet Vela r 1.244, ν 73.9, v 33.75; day 500 Comet Vela r 4.359, ν 156.0, v 10.99; day 0 Earth r 0.983, ν 0.0, v 30.29. For R7 jump to days 0, 60, 900 and 1000 and compare the comet's position and ν. Press Escape to close the panel. You may use eval to read the panel's text.

rubric.criterion: The Sun sits at a focus of six drawn elliptical orbits (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Comet Vela), each with its body on it; the comet's orbit is a clearly elongated ellipse with the Sun near one end rather than at its centre, and Jupiter is the largest planet on the largest planetary orbit.
The HUD shows 'Kepler Lab' with a 'Day N.N' readout, a Play/Pause button, '1×', '10×' and '100×' speed buttons, a 'Day' scrubber, and a 'Jump to day' input with a 'Go' button.

Time runs on load at about 10 days per second (the Day readout grows by roughly 15 over 1.5 s), '100×' makes it about ten times faster, and Pause stops both the readout and all motion until Play is pressed.
After jumping to day 500 and selecting Mars, the panel shows 'Period 687.2 d', r = 1.556 AU, ν = 251.6° and v = 23.61 km/s (each within 1 unit of the last shown digit).

Comet Vela is correct at two times: at day 60 the panel shows r = 1.244 AU, ν = 73.9°, v = 33.75 km/s, and at day 500 r = 4.359 AU, ν = 156.0°, v = 10.99 km/s (each within 1 unit of the last shown digit); its period reads 1993.6 d.
At day 0 Earth's panel shows r = 0.983 AU, ν = 0.0° and v = 30.29 km/s, and every body sits at the point of its orbit closest to the Sun (each perihelion lies in a different direction).

Kepler's second law is visible: the comet sweeps a large arc near the Sun (about 74° of ν between day 0 and day 60) but barely moves near aphelion (about 4° between day 900 and day 1000), and its tail points away from the Sun at every position checked.
Clicking a body adds a highlight ring and opens its panel, the panel values change while time is running, and clicking empty space or pressing Escape closes it.
With 'Follow' checked the selected body stays centred while time runs; dragging orbits the camera and the wheel zooms.
In the initial view the whole of Jupiter's and the comet's orbits fit inside the 1280x720 frame, and the title, time bar and panel do not overlap each other or cover the Sun.
The Sun visibly glows, planets are shaded with their lit side facing the Sun, a starfield fills the background, and the HUD uses one consistent typeface with aligned, legible numbers.

title: Gridwork: seeded procedural city with a sun path
prompt:
Build 'Gridwork', a deterministic procedural city generator in three.js. The same seed must always produce the same city, so follow these rules exactly.

Layout: a 13 × 13 grid of 10 m cells, columns c = 0–12 running west to east (+X) and rows r = 0–12 running north to south (+Z), centred on the origin. A cell is road if c % 4 == 0 or r % 4 == 0, which leaves 9 blocks of 3 × 3 lots (81 lots). Roads are dark asphalt with dashed centre lines. Draw large N, E, S and W letters on the ground just outside the four edges of the city.

Generation uses this PRNG:
function mulberry32(a) { return function () { a |= 0; a = a + 0x6D2B79F5 | 0; let t = Math.imul(a ^ a >>> 15, 1 | a); t = t + Math.imul(t ^ t >>> 7, 61 | t) ^ t; return ((t ^ t >>> 14) >>> 0) / 4294967296; }; }
Create rand = mulberry32(seed) and visit the lots in row-major order (r from 0 to 12, and within a row c from 0 to 12, skipping roads). For each lot draw u1 = rand(): if u1 < 0.12 the lot is a park (grass and one tree) and nothing else is drawn for it. Otherwise draw u2 = rand() and set floors = 2 + floor(u2 × u2 × 18); lots in the central block (c and r both between 5 and 7) get 10 extra floors. Each building is an 8 × 8 m box centred in its lot, floors × 3.2 m tall, with rows of windows, coloured by floors: up to 5 sandstone #e8d5b7, 6–12 slate blue #9fb4c7, 13 or more glass teal #5fa8a0.

Panel (top-left): a 'Seed' number input (default 2026) with a 'Generate' button (Enter also works), and live stats: 'Buildings', 'Parks', 'Tallest' (as '17 floors · 54.4 m') and 'Mean height' (the mean building height in metres, parks excluded, one decimal).

Sun and time: a 'Time' slider from 0 to 24 h in 0.25 h steps (default 10:00) with an HH:MM readout, and a 'Play day' toggle that advances one hour per second and wraps at 24:00. The sun's elevation is 60° × sin(π·(h − 6)/12) and its azimuth is 90° + 15°·(h − 6), clockwise from north (east at 06:00, south at noon, west at 18:00). Show it as 'Sun E° elev · A° az' with one decimal each. A shadow-casting directional light comes from that direction. When the elevation is below 0° it is night: dark sky with stars, lit windows, and street lamps glowing along the roads.

Picking: clicking a building highlights it and shows 'Lot (c, r) · N floors · H m'; clicking a park shows 'Lot (c, r) · Park'.

Camera: orbit and zoom, starting from a high view from the south-east that shows the whole city.
interaction_hints: Default seed 2026 must show Buildings 66, Parks 15, Tallest 28 floors · 89.6 m, Mean height 29.8 m. Type 42 into the Seed input (type with its selector) and click Generate (or press Enter): Buildings 69, Parks 12, Tallest 29 floors · 92.8 m, Mean height 29.0 m. Then generate 2026 again and compare with the first screenshot. In seed 2026 the 28-floor tower is on lot (6, 6), the centre lot of the city. Set the Time slider with type on its selector (values 9, 15.5, 22, 12) or with eval (set .value and dispatch input and change events) and judge shadow directions against the N/E/S/W ground letters. Click Play day and take screenshots 1 s apart.

rubric.criterion: The city is a 13 × 13 cell grid with roads on every fourth row and column forming 9 blocks of 3 × 3 lots; buildings are separate boxes set back inside their lots, parks are green lots with a tree, roads have dashed centre lines, and N, E, S, W letters sit outside the city edges.
For the default seed 2026 the stats read exactly Buildings 66, Parks 15, Tallest 28 floors · 89.6 m, and Mean height 29.8 m.

Generating seed 42 gives exactly Buildings 69, Parks 12, Tallest 29 floors · 92.8 m and Mean height 29.0 m, and generating 2026 again reproduces the original city (same stats and the same buildings in a screenshot).
The central block of 3 × 3 lots is clearly the tallest cluster, and building colours follow the floor bands (sandstone for low, slate blue for mid-rise, teal for 13+ floors).
For seed 2026, clicking the tallest building shows 'Lot (6, 6) · 28 floors · 89.6 m' (the lot at the very centre of the city) and highlights it; clicking a park lot shows that it is a park.

At 09:00 the readout shows 'Sun 42.4° elev · 135.0° az' and shadows fall toward the north-west (away from the south-east sun, judged against the ground letters); at 15:30 it shows 36.5° elev · 232.5° az and shadows fall toward the north-east.
At 22:00 it is night (dark sky with stars, lit windows, glowing street lamps), and moving back to 12:00 restores full daylight.
'Play day' advances the clock about one hour per second, with the readout, sun and shadows moving continuously, and wraps from 23:xx to 00:xx.
Dragging orbits the camera around the city and the wheel zooms.
The initial view from the south-east shows the whole city inside the frame, and the panel does not cover the central block.
Buildings show readable window rows, daytime shadows are crisp without visible acne or striping, and the night mode has a coherent dark palette with warm lights.

title: MolView: XYZ molecule viewer with bond detection and measurement
prompt:
Build 'MolView', a three.js molecule viewer for a chemistry course, driven by the two attached files caffeine.xyz and paracetamol.xyz (standard XYZ format: the atom count, a title line, then one 'Element x y z' line per atom, in ångströms). Do not hard-code the molecules: copy the files next to your page, parse them at runtime and derive everything from the coordinates.

Rules:
- Atom labels are the element symbol plus the 1-based position of the atom in the file (O1, O2, N3, …).
- Bonds: connect two atoms when their distance is at most 1.15 × (r1 + r2), with covalent radii H 0.31, C 0.76, N 0.71 and O 0.66 Å. Draw each bond as two half-cylinders coloured like the atom at each end.
- Colours: C #505050, H #ffffff, N #3050f8, O #ff0d0d.
- Molar mass uses H 1.008, C 12.011, N 14.007 and O 15.999, shown with 3 decimals as '123.456 g/mol'. The formula uses Hill order (C first, then H, then the other elements alphabetically) with subscript digits.

UI:
- A 'Molecule' dropdown with Caffeine and Paracetamol (Caffeine loads first). Switching rebuilds the scene and re-frames the camera so the molecule is centred and seen face-on.
- An info card with the file's title line, the formula, the molar mass and 'Atoms N · Bonds M'.
- Style buttons 'Ball & stick' (default), 'Space-filling' (spheres at van der Waals radii H 1.20, C 1.70, N 1.55, O 1.52 Å, no bonds) and 'Sticks'.
- Toggles 'Labels' (atom labels next to each atom, always facing the camera) and 'Hide H' (hides hydrogens and their bonds; the card then reads, for example, 'Atoms 30 (18 shown)').
- An atom list with one row per atom: label, element and coordinates.
- Picking: clicking an atom in the 3D view or its row in the list selects it with a glowing halo and shows its label, element name, coordinates (3 decimals) and bonded neighbours in file order, e.g. 'Bonded to: C4, H9'.
- A 'Measure' toggle: in this mode, picking two atoms (in the view or the list) shows their distance as 'C4–H9: 1.090 Å' with a dashed line between them, and a third atom shows the angle at the middle atom with 1 decimal. Escape clears the measurement.
- Drag to rotate, wheel to zoom, and an 'Auto-rotate' toggle (off by default).

Use lighting that makes the spheres look glossy and three-dimensional against a dark background.
interaction_hints: The input files are in /grader/task/. Select atoms through the atom list rows (easiest) or by clicking in the 3D view with Labels on. Caffeine: title 'Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine)', C8H10N4O2, 194.194 g/mol, Atoms 24 · Bonds 25; C12 is bonded to N3, H16, H17, H18; N6 to C8 and C11 only. Turn on Measure and pick O1 then C7: 1.230 Å; pick C11, N5, C9 (in that order): 108.0°. Switch the Molecule dropdown (select action) to Paracetamol: C8H9NO2, 151.165 g/mol, Atoms 20 · Bonds 20; measure C10, N3, C7: 128.0°. Hide H on Caffeine must read 'Atoms 24 (14 shown)'. Drag from (640,360) to (800,360) to rotate.

rubric.criterion: Caffeine loads first as a ball-and-stick model with 24 atoms in the specified colours: a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring, two oxygens and three methyl groups, with bonds drawn as two half-cylinders coloured by their atoms.
The Caffeine card shows the title 'Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine)', the formula C8H10N4O2 with subscript digits, '194.194 g/mol' and 'Atoms 24 · Bonds 25'.
Switching to Paracetamol rebuilds and re-frames the scene (a benzene ring with an OH group and an acetamide group) and the card shows C8H9NO2, '151.165 g/mol' and 'Atoms 20 · Bonds 20'.
Bond detection is correct: in Caffeine, selecting C12 lists exactly N3, H16, H17 and H18 as bonded neighbours, and selecting N6 lists exactly C8 and C11.
Measurements are exact: Caffeine O1–C7 reads 1.230 Å, the angle C11–N5–C9 reads 108.0°, and in Paracetamol the angle C10–N3–C7 reads 128.0°.
Clicking an atom directly in the 3D view selects that atom (halo plus a matching info panel), and clicking a list row selects the same atom in the view.
'Labels' shows readable labels O1, O2, N3 … in file order next to the right atoms, and they stay upright and facing the camera after rotating.
'Hide H' removes the hydrogens and their bonds and the Caffeine card reads 'Atoms 24 (14 shown)'; turning it off restores them.
'Space-filling' shows large overlapping spheres with no bonds, 'Sticks' shows a thin stick model, and 'Ball & stick' restores the default.
Dragging rotates the molecule, the wheel zooms, and 'Auto-rotate' spins it continuously until turned off.
The initial view shows the whole molecule centred and face-on (not edge-on), and the card, style buttons and atom list do not cover it; the list scrolls instead of overflowing the page.
Spheres are smoothly shaded with specular highlights against a dark background, and the panels share one clean, legible style.

title: Terraform: heightfield editor with contours and water
prompt:
Build 'Terraform', a small terrain editor in three.js.

Terrain: a 128 m × 128 m heightfield centred on the origin, sampled as a 129 × 129 vertex grid (1 m spacing, x and z from −64 to 64). The initial height in metres is
h(x, z) = 18·exp(−((x − 20)² + (z + 12)²)/500) + 11·exp(−((x + 26)² + (z − 18)²)/350) + 4·sin(x/9)·cos(z/11) + 1
Tint it by height, blending smoothly: below 0 m sand #d9c89e, 0–4 m light green #9cc47a, 4–10 m forest green #4f8a4b, 10–16 m rock #8a7560, above 16 m snow #f4f4f0. Overlay contour lines: a thin dark line every 2 m of height and a thicker one every 10 m. They must follow the terrain as it is edited, so compute them per pixel in a shader from the height rather than baking a texture once.

Water: a semi-transparent blue plane at the height of a 'Water level' slider (−5 to 20 m, step 0.5, default 1 m).

Tools: a toolbar with 'Raise', 'Lower', 'Flatten' and 'Camera' (keys 1–4). With a sculpt tool active, a ring cursor of the brush radius follows the terrain under the mouse (raycasting); a click applies one dab and dragging applies a dab every 2 m of cursor travel. A dab changes each vertex within distance d < R of the hit point by S·(1 − (d/R)²)², added for Raise and subtracted for Lower; Flatten moves each vertex toward the height at the hit point by half the difference times the same falloff. Sliders: 'Radius' 2–20 m (default 8) and 'Strength' 0.5–5 m (default 2). With 'Camera' active, dragging orbits; the wheel always zooms. Normals and contours update immediately.

Status bar, updated after every dab and slider change:
- the cursor readout 'x 12.0  z −8.0  h 7.43 m' for the terrain point under the mouse;
- 'Min −1.25 m · Max 18.40 m' over all vertices (2 decimals);
- 'Water coverage 42.0%': the share of vertices strictly below the water level, 1 decimal.

History: Ctrl+Z undoes the last stroke (a whole drag is one stroke), up to 20 strokes, and a 'Reset terrain' button restores the initial heights.
interaction_hints: At load the status must read Min −2.99 m · Max 21.03 m and Water coverage 28.4%. Set the Water level slider (type with its selector and a value, or eval: set .value and dispatch input and change events) to 4 (69.2%), 0 (14.7%) and back to 1 (28.4%). Select Raise (click or press 1), move the mouse over a terrain point and read h, click there once, move away and back to the same pixel and read h again (about +2 m); take screenshots. Do a drag stroke with Raise, then press Control+z and compare the stats with the values before the stroke. Click Reset terrain. Press 4 (Camera) and drag to confirm orbiting; press 1 and drag to confirm it sculpts instead.

rubric.criterion: The initial terrain matches the formula: one tall main peak with a snow cap, a lower second peak (rock-coloured, no snow), rolling ripples elsewhere and low basins partly under water, tinted by height from sand through greens and rock to snow.
At load the status bar reads 'Min −2.99 m · Max 21.03 m' and 'Water coverage 28.4%'.
Setting the water level to 4 m gives 'Water coverage 69.2%' and 0 m gives 14.7%, with the water plane visibly rising and falling.
Contour lines are visible: thin lines every 2 m and a visibly thicker line every 10 m, following the terrain shape; after sculpting they bend around the new bump.

With Raise, one click makes a smooth round bump about the brush radius wide and the h readout at that spot rises by about the strength (1.5–2.2 m at default settings); Lower digs a matching dent; Min, Max and coverage update after the dab.
Flatten visibly levels the area under the brush toward the height at the clicked point, and changing Radius changes both the ring cursor size and the affected area.
A ring cursor follows the terrain under the mouse in sculpt mode and the x/z/h readout updates as the mouse moves.
Ctrl+Z undoes a whole drag stroke at once and the Min, Max and coverage values return exactly to their previous values; 'Reset terrain' restores −2.99 m, 21.03 m and 28.4%.
With 'Camera' active dragging orbits the view, while with a sculpt tool active dragging sculpts instead of orbiting; the wheel zooms in both.
The initial view shows the whole terrain square inside the frame, and the toolbar, sliders and status bar do not overlap each other.
Lighting shows the relief clearly (lit slopes versus shaded slopes), colour bands blend without harsh stripes, and the contour lines are crisp and even in width.

title: CubeLab: Rubik's cube with notation, seeded scrambles and a net
prompt:
Build 'CubeLab', a 3x3 Rubik's cube simulator in three.js that follows standard notation exactly.

Cube: 27 dark rounded cubies (RoundedBoxGeometry) with slightly inset stickers on the outer faces only. Solved orientation: white Up, yellow Down, green Front, blue Back, red Right, orange Left. The camera shows the Up, Front and Right faces in a three-quarter view; dragging on empty space orbits and the wheel zooms.

Notation: a text field with an 'Apply' button (Enter also applies). Tokens are separated by spaces: face turns U D L R F B (clockwise when looking straight at that face), slice moves M (the layer between L and R, turning like L), E (between U and D, turning like D) and S (between F and B, turning like F), and whole-cube rotations x (like R), y (like U) and z (like F). Any token may end with ' (counter-clockwise) or 2 (half turn). If any token is invalid, nothing is applied and an error such as 'Unknown move: K' appears under the field. The letter keys U D L R F B M E S X Y Z (either case) do the same as single tokens, and Shift makes them counter-clockwise.

Animation: every turn animates in about 200 ms; tokens arriving while a turn is animating are queued, so long sequences play through without losing a move or leaving pieces misaligned.

Counting: 'Moves: N' counts in the half-turn metric (a half turn counts once; x, y and z do not count). A history strip lists the applied tokens, and 'Undo' (also Ctrl+Z) reverses the last token and removes it from the count and the history. 'Reset' returns to the solved cube.

Solved detection: whenever every face is a single colour (in any orientation) after at least one counted move, show a 'Solved!' badge with the move count and the time since the timer started. The timer starts at the first move after a scramble or reset.

Seeded scramble: a 'Seed' number input and a 'Scramble' button. Use this PRNG:
function mulberry32(a) { return function () { a |= 0; a = a + 0x6D2B79F5 | 0; let t = Math.imul(a ^ a >>> 15, 1 | a); t = t + Math.imul(t ^ t >>> 7, 61 | t) ^ t; return ((t ^ t >>> 14) >>> 0) / 4294967296; }; }
With rand = mulberry32(seed), generate 20 moves. For each move pick face = 'UDLRFB'[floor(rand() × 6)], drawing again while it equals the previous move's face; then pick the suffix with floor(rand() × 3): 0 for none, 1 for prime ('), 2 for a half turn (2). Show the scramble text, apply it instantly from the solved state, and reset the move counter and the timer.

Net: a 2D unfolded net in a corner (Up above Front; Left, Front, Right and Back in a row; Down below Front) that always matches the 3D cube.
interaction_hints: Use the notation field (type with its selector, then press Enter or click Apply) and click Reset between checks; wait about 250 ms per queued token before screenshots. From solved: R → Up right column green, Front right column yellow; U → Front top row red; M → Front middle column white; x → green on top, yellow in front, Moves stays 0; M2 E2 S2 → checkerboards. Enter R U R' U' repeated 6 times (24 tokens), wait about 7 s: Solved! and Moves: 24. Type 7 into the Seed input and click Scramble: the scramble text must be exactly U B2 R' L R2 D F' D' R B D U R2 U2 R' F2 R2 F D' L and the Front face Y R R / Y G W / O O W (Y yellow, R red, G green, W white, O orange). Then apply L' D F' R2 F2 R U2 R2 U' D' B' R' D F D' R2 L' R B2 U' → Solved!, Moves: 20. R U K must be rejected. Keyboard: press r for R and Shift+R for R'; Control+z undoes.

rubric.criterion: The cube is 27 dark rounded cubies with inset stickers on the outer faces only, solved with white on top, green in front and red on the right, shown in a three-quarter view of the Up, Front and Right faces.
Face turns go the right way: from solved, 'R' makes the right column of the Up face green and the right column of the Front face yellow; from solved, 'U' makes the top row of the Front face red.

Slices and rotations are correct: from solved, 'M' makes the middle column of the Front face white; 'x' puts green on top and yellow in front and leaves 'Moves: 0'; 'M2 E2 S2' produces a checkerboard on every face.
Entering ‘R U R' U'’ six times in a row (24 tokens) from solved ends aligned and solved, showing 'Solved!' with 'Moves: 24'; after only five repetitions the cube is not solved.

Seed 7 produces exactly the scramble ‘U B2 R' L R2 D F' D' R B D U R2 U2 R' F2 R2 F D' L’, after which the Front face reads (top row first, left to right) yellow red red / yellow green white / orange orange white.
After the seed 7 scramble, applying the inverse ‘L' D F' R2 F2 R U2 R2 U' D' B' R' D F D' R2 L' R B2 U'’ solves the cube and shows 'Solved!' with 'Moves: 20'.
Entering ‘R U K’ shows an error naming K and applies nothing ('Moves' and the cube stay unchanged).
Turns animate (a screenshot right after a move shows a partly rotated layer) and quickly entered moves are queued without misalignment.
'Undo' or Ctrl+Z reverses the last token and decrements 'Moves'; pressing the r key turns R and Shift+R turns R'.
The 2D net shows all 54 stickers in the cross layout and matches the 3D cube after moves and after a scramble.
The cube sits centred without overlapping the notation field, history strip, net or buttons, and all labels are legible.

title: Gravity Ribbon: spline marble run with checkpoints
prompt:
Build 'Gravity Ribbon', a marble-run visualiser in three.js. There is no physics engine: the marble moves along a fixed spline and its speed comes from energy conservation.

Track: a THREE.CatmullRomCurve3 (open, centripetal) through these 16 control points P0–P15, in metres with y up:
(−9, 12, −6), (−4, 11.4, −7), (2, 10.4, −6), (6, 9.2, −3), (6.5, 8.2, 2), (2, 7.2, 5), (−4, 6.2, 5.5), (−8, 5.2, 2), (−7, 4.4, −3), (−2, 3.6, −4), (3, 2.8, −2), (4, 2.2, 2), (0, 1.6, 3), (−4, 1.1, 1), (−3, 0.8, −1.5), (2, 0.6, −0.5).
Build it as a U-shaped channel or twin rails with cross ties that follow the curve, carried by thin vertical support posts every 2 m of arc length down to a ground plane at y = 0.

Motion: the marble (radius 0.25 m, glossy, with a stripe or pattern so its rolling is visible) starts at P0 with v0 = 1.5 m/s and advances along the curve by arc length s with ds/dt = v, where v = √(v0² + 2·9.81·(12 − y)) and y is its current height. It rolls without slipping: its spin angle equals the distance travelled divided by its radius.

Checkpoints: gates labelled CP1, CP2 and CP3 at P4, P8 and P12, and a FINISH arch at P15. When the marble passes a gate, the gate turns green and a split row is added, formatted 'CP1 · 0.00 s · 0.00 m/s' (simulation time since release and speed at the gate). Times are interpolated to the exact crossing, so they do not depend on the frame rate.

HUD: 'Release', 'Pause'/'Resume' and 'Reset' buttons; a 'Slow motion' toggle that plays at 0.25× real time while producing identical splits; readouts for speed (m/s, 2 decimals), height (m, 2 decimals) and distance as 's 12.3 / L m' where L is the total track length (1 decimal); and a progress bar. At the finish show 'Run complete' with the finish time.

Cameras (buttons or keys 1–3): 'Chase' follows behind and above the marble, looking along its direction of travel with smoothing; 'Overview' (the default) is a fixed wide shot of the whole track in which dragging orbits; 'Top' is an orthographic top-down view.
interaction_hints: Click Release and wait 11000 ms, then screenshot: splits should be CP1 4.73 s · 8.76 m/s, CP2 6.88 s · 12.30 m/s, CP3 8.34 s · 14.36 m/s, FINISH 9.20 s · 15.03 m/s (times ±0.10 s, speeds ±0.02). If the run has not finished (slow software rendering), wait longer. Screenshot around 2 s and 5 s after Release to see the readouts and the marble in flight. Then in a fresh page: click Slow motion, click Release, wait 21000 ms: CP1 must equal the normal-speed CP1 and the run must not be finished. Test Pause with two screenshots 1000 ms apart, then Resume. Press 1, 2 and 3 (or click Chase, Overview, Top) and screenshot each.

rubric.criterion: The track is one smooth, continuous spline that winds down from a high start to a low end as a channel or twin rails with cross ties, standing on vertical support posts down to a ground plane, with gates labelled CP1, CP2, CP3 and a FINISH arch.
The HUD has Release, Pause/Resume, Reset and Slow motion controls, speed and height readouts, a progress bar and a distance readout whose total length is 76.7 m (±0.1).

After Release the splits read CP1 4.73 s · 8.76 m/s, CP2 6.88 s · 12.30 m/s, CP3 8.34 s · 14.36 m/s and FINISH 9.20 s · 15.03 m/s (times within ±0.10 s, speeds within ±0.02 m/s), and 'Run complete' appears.
Before release the speed reads 1.50 m/s and the height 12.00 m; during the run the speed only grows as the marble descends and the height ends at 0.60 m.
With 'Slow motion' on, the run is clearly slower in real time (CP1 is reached after roughly 19 s) but the CP1 split equals the normal-speed split within 0.02 s.
Pause freezes the marble and all readouts (two screenshots a second apart are identical), and Resume continues from the same place.
Passed gates turn green and split rows appear in order CP1, CP2, CP3, FINISH; Reset returns the marble to the start, clears the splits and restores the gate colours.
The marble stays in the channel or on the rails for the whole run and visibly rolls in the direction of travel.
'Chase' follows behind the marble looking along the track, 'Overview' shows the whole track and can be orbited by dragging, and 'Top' is a top-down orthographic view.
In the default Overview the whole track fits in the frame and the HUD panels (buttons, readouts, splits) do not overlap each other or hide the track.
The marble is glossy with visible reflections or highlights, the track and supports cast shadows on the ground, and gates and HUD share a consistent colour scheme.

title: Roomy: room planner with grid snapping and collisions
prompt:
Build 'Roomy', a 3D room planner in three.js.

Room: a floor 6.0 m wide (x from 0 at the left to 6 at the right) and 4.5 m deep (z from 0 at the back wall to 4.5 at the front), with 2.6 m tall back and left walls; the front and right walls are low 0.1 m curbs so the camera can see in. Draw 0.5 m grid lines on the floor. All positions below are the footprint's minimum corner (x, z) in metres.

Catalog (a sidebar of buttons; width along x × depth along z at 0°): Bed 2.0 × 1.6, Desk 1.2 × 0.6, Wardrobe 1.0 × 0.6, Sofa 2.0 × 0.9, Bookshelf 0.8 × 0.3, Armchair 0.8 × 0.8, Plant 0.5 × 0.5 and Rug 2.0 × 1.5. Model each from a few primitives so it is recognisable (the bed has a headboard and pillow, the plant a pot and foliage, the rug is flat).

Rules:
- Adding: clicking a catalog button places the item at 0° at the first free position found by scanning z = 0, 0.5, 1.0, … and, for each z, x = 0, 0.5, 1.0, …. A position is free when the footprint stays inside the room and does not overlap another item's footprint (touching edges is allowed). If nothing fits, show 'No space for Bed' with the item's name and add nothing.
- Rugs lie under furniture: they ignore collisions (only the room bounds apply) and do not count as occupied area.
- Moving: drag an item across the floor (raycast onto the floor plane). While dragging, it snaps so its corner sits on the 0.5 m grid; if the snapped spot is invalid, the item turns red, and on release it returns to its last valid position. Dragging empty space orbits the camera.
- Rotating: R or a Rotate button turns the selected item 90° clockwise seen from above, keeping its minimum corner fixed; if the rotated footprint would be invalid, show 'Can't rotate here' and leave it unchanged.
- Selecting: click an item in the room (it gets an outline or highlight); Delete or Backspace removes it; Ctrl+Z undoes the last add, move, rotate or delete.

Panel: the placed items in placement order, each row as 'Desk — x 2.0, z 0.0, 0°' (clicking a row selects the item), and a summary 'Items N · Occupied A m² (P%)', where A is the total footprint area of all non-rug items (2 decimals) and P its share of the 27.00 m² floor (1 decimal). The layout persists in localStorage and is restored on reload; a 'Clear room' button empties it.

A 'Plan view' toggle switches to a top-down orthographic camera that shows the dimension labels '6.0 m' and '4.5 m' along the walls.
interaction_hints: Start from a fresh page; if a layout is restored, click Clear room. Click the catalog buttons Bed, Desk, Wardrobe, Sofa in order: rows Bed x 0.0, z 0.0; Desk x 2.0, z 0.0; Wardrobe x 3.5, z 0.0; Sofa x 2.0, z 1.0; summary Items 4 · Occupied 6.32 m² (23.4%). Add Rug: x 0.0, z 0.0, area unchanged, Items 5. Click the Desk row and press r: Can't rotate here. Click the Bed row and press r: 90°. For dragging, locate an item in a screenshot and drag it onto another item (it must return) and onto empty floor (it must snap). Press Delete, then Control+z. Use reload to check persistence. Then Clear room and click Bed seven times: six beds, No space for Bed, Items 6 · Occupied 19.20 m² (71.1%). Toggle Plan view.

rubric.criterion: The room is a 6.0 × 4.5 m floor with 0.5 m grid lines, tall back and left walls and low front and right curbs, next to a catalog of the eight items.

Adding Bed, Desk, Wardrobe and Sofa in that order to an empty room lists Bed x 0.0, z 0.0; Desk x 2.0, z 0.0; Wardrobe x 3.5, z 0.0; Sofa x 2.0, z 1.0 (all 0°), the 3D pieces sit at those spots, and the summary reads 'Items 4 · Occupied 6.32 m² (23.4%)'.
Adding a Rug next places it at x 0.0, z 0.0 overlapping the bed, and the summary becomes 'Items 5' with the occupied area still 6.32 m² (23.4%).

Rotation follows the rules: with that layout, rotating the Desk shows 'Can't rotate here' and changes nothing, while rotating the Bed turns it to 90° (row 'Bed — x 0.0, z 0.0, 90°') with a 1.6 m wide, 2.0 m deep footprint.
Dragging an item moves it in 0.5 m snapped steps; dragging it onto another item turns it red and on release it jumps back to its last valid spot, so items never overlap or leave the room.
Adding Bed seven times to an empty room places six beds (x 0.0, 2.0 and 4.0 at z 0.0 and at z 2.0), then shows 'No space for Bed', and the summary reads 'Items 6 · Occupied 19.20 m² (71.1%)'.
Delete removes the selected item and updates the list and summary; Ctrl+Z brings it back in the same place.
Reloading the page restores the same layout from localStorage, and 'Clear room' empties it.
'Plan view' switches to a top-down orthographic view with the labels '6.0 m' and '4.5 m' along the walls and can be switched back.
The furniture is recognisable (bed with headboard and pillow, desk, wardrobe, sofa with back and arms, bookshelf, armchair, potted plant, flat rug) and the selected item is clearly highlighted.
The catalog, list and summary panels do not overlap the room or each other, and the list stays readable with a dozen items.

title: Rain Atlas: 3D bar chart from a CSV
prompt:
Turn the attached rainfall.csv (monthly rainfall in mm at six weather stations) into 'Rain Atlas', an interactive 3D bar chart in three.js. Copy the CSV next to your page and parse it at runtime; do not hard-code values.

Chart:
- A 12 × 6 grid of bars on a base plate: months along X (Jan to Dec) and stations along Z in file order. Bar height is proportional to rainfall on one shared scale. Colour bars along a sequential ramp from pale teal at 0 mm to deep indigo at the largest value, with a legend colour bar labelled with 0 and that largest value.
- A value axis with ticks and labels every 50 mm from 0 to 250 mm and faint horizontal gridlines on a back wall; month labels along the front edge and station names along the side, all readable from the default camera.
- An empty cell means no reading: draw a short grey translucent stub there, show 'no data' in its tooltip, and exclude it from every total, mean and count. A reading of 0 is a real value: draw a flat tile and show '0 mm'.

Interaction:
- Hovering a bar highlights it and shows a tooltip such as 'Ridge · Mar · 118 mm'.
- A side panel lists every station with its annual total, and shows 'Wettest month overall: Mon (N mm)' for the month with the largest total across all stations, plus 'Mean of all readings: X.X mm (N readings)'.
- A 'Sort stations' select with 'File order' and 'Annual total' (descending): the rows animate to their new positions and their labels move with them.
- Clicking a station name in the panel isolates its row (the other bars fade to about 20% opacity); clicking it again shows all rows.
- A 'Threshold' slider (0–250 mm, step 10): bars below it fade out and a counter reads 'N of M readings ≥ T mm'.
- Camera buttons 'Front', 'Top' and 'Iso' (the default) animate the camera smoothly, and dragging orbits.
interaction_hints: The CSV is at /grader/task/rainfall.csv. Click Top first to make bars easy to target, then hover bars (hover with x,y from a screenshot): Harbor Nov 212 mm (tallest), Lakeside Jul 104 mm, Dunes Jul 0 mm, Ridge Jul no data. Panel totals: Harbor 1298, Ridge 1128, Northpoint 1026, Lakeside 917, Mill Valley 651, Dunes 164; Wettest month overall: Nov (654 mm); Mean of all readings: 73.0 mm (71 readings). Set Threshold (type with its selector, or eval plus input/change events) to 100 → 16 of 71, and 150 → 3 of 71. Use the select action on the Sort stations select and screenshot during and after the animation. Click a station name in the panel twice.

rubric.criterion: A 12 × 6 grid of bars with heights proportional to the CSV values: Harbor's November bar is the tallest, the Dunes row is almost flat, and month labels (Jan–Dec) and station names are placed on the correct rows and columns.
A value axis shows ticks labelled 0, 50, 100, 150, 200 and 250 mm with faint gridlines, and bars are coloured on a teal-to-indigo ramp with a legend labelled 0 and 212.
Tooltips show exact values: Harbor · Nov · 212 mm, Lakeside · Jul · 104 mm, and Dunes · Jul · 0 mm (drawn as a flat tile), with the hovered bar highlighted.
The missing Ridge July reading is a grey translucent stub whose tooltip says 'no data'.

The panel totals are exactly Harbor 1298, Ridge 1128, Northpoint 1026, Lakeside 917, Mill Valley 651 and Dunes 164 mm, with 'Wettest month overall: Nov (654 mm)' and 'Mean of all readings: 73.0 mm (71 readings)'.
Sorting by 'Annual total' reorders the rows to Harbor, Ridge, Northpoint, Lakeside, Mill Valley, Dunes with an animation and the labels moving along; 'File order' restores the CSV order.
Setting the threshold to 100 shows '16 of 71 readings ≥ 100 mm' and to 150 shows '3 of 71 readings ≥ 150 mm', with the bars below the threshold faded.
Clicking a station name isolates its row (others fade), and clicking it again restores all rows.
'Front', 'Top' and 'Iso' move the camera smoothly to the matching views, and dragging orbits.
In the default view the whole chart, its labels and the legend fit in the frame without overlapping the side panel, and axis labels do not collide with each other.
The chart looks like a polished data visualisation: soft lighting and shadows that keep bar colours readable, a clear colour ramp, and consistent label typography.

title: Lantern Maze: first-person maze with key, door and minimap
prompt:
Build 'Lantern Maze', a first-person maze game in three.js, from the attached maze.txt: 13 lines of 13 characters where # is a wall, . is floor, S is the start, K is a key, D is a locked door and E is the exit. The first line is the north edge, so rows grow southward and columns grow eastward. Copy the file next to your page and parse it at runtime.

World: each character is a 2 m cell. Walls are 2.5 m tall with a stone or brick texture drawn on a canvas, and the maze has a floor and a ceiling. The player carries a warm lantern (a point light at the camera) and corridors fade into darkness or fog. The key floats and slowly spins, the door is a wooden door that swings or slides open, and the exit is a glowing portal.

Movement is grid-based: the player starts on S facing north. W or ArrowUp moves one cell forward, S or ArrowDown one cell back, A and D strafe one cell left and right, and Q/E or ArrowLeft/ArrowRight turn 90°. Letter keys work in either case. Every step or turn animates smoothly in about 150 ms, and keys pressed during an animation are queued and executed in order. Moving into a wall does not move the player: it plays a short bump shake and increments 'Bumps'. The door blocks like a wall and shows 'The door is locked' until the key has been collected; walking onto K collects it and lights a key icon in the HUD. After that, stepping into the door opens it for good and moves the player onto its cell in the same step.

HUD:
- 'Steps N' (successful moves only; turns and bumps do not count), 'Bumps N', a compass showing the facing (N, E, S or W) and the position as 'Cell (col, row)', 0-based as in the file.
- A minimap in the top-right that shows only revealed cells (a cell is revealed once the player has stood on it or on one of its 8 neighbours), the player as an arrow pointing in the facing direction, and K, D and E as icons once revealed.
- A 'Hint' button (also H) that draws the shortest route on the minimap (through the key first if it has not been collected) and shows 'Route: N steps'.

Reaching E shows an 'Escaped!' panel with the steps, bumps and time, and a 'Play again' button (also R) that restarts everything.
interaction_hints: The maze file is at /grader/task/maze.txt. Press lowercase keys (w, a, s, d, q, e, h, r). Each step animates about 150 ms, so after a sequence wait about 200 ms per queued key before a screenshot. Start: Cell (1, 11) facing N. w×8 then wait: Cell (1, 3), Steps 8; then a: Bumps 1, same cell. Click Hint (or press h) at the start: Route: 48 steps. Full solution from a fresh page, keeping the facing north (strafing): w×8, d×2, w×2, a×2 (key at Cell (1, 1)), d×10, s×2, a×2, s×4, a×2, s×4, d×4, w×6 → Escaped! with 48 steps and 0 bumps (wait about 10 s). Locked door from a fresh page: w×8, d×2, w×2, d×8, s×2, a×2, s×4, a×2, s×4, d×4, w×3 reaches Cell (11, 8); one more w shows The door is locked. Press r to restart.

rubric.criterion: The 3D maze matches maze.txt: textured walls, floor and ceiling, and the first view from S at Cell (1, 11) facing N looks up a long corridor to the north.
The lantern lights nearby walls warmly and corridors fade into darkness or fog; the key floats and spins, the door looks like a door, and the exit is a glowing portal.
Movement is exact: from the start, pressing w eight times reaches Cell (1, 3) with Steps 8; pressing a there (a wall to the west) shakes the view, increments Bumps to 1 and leaves the cell unchanged.
Q/E or the arrow keys turn the view 90° with the compass updating, and after turning to face east, w moves the player east.
Hint from the start shows 'Route: 48 steps' and draws the route on the minimap through the key.
Following the route from the start without turning (w×8, d×2, w×2, a×2, d×10, s×2, a×2, s×4, a×2, s×4, d×4, w×6) collects the key, opens the door and shows 'Escaped!' with 48 steps and 0 bumps.
Without the key the door stays shut: after w×8, d×2, w×2, d×8, s×2, a×2, s×4, a×2, s×4, d×4, w×3 the player is at Cell (11, 8), and one more w shows 'The door is locked' without moving.
The minimap reveals only cells around places the player has stood, with the arrow pointing in the facing direction, and shows K, D and E icons once revealed.
Picking up the key lights the HUD key icon, and the door visibly animates open when entered with the key.
'Play again' or R restarts: Steps 0, Bumps 0, Cell (1, 11) facing N, the minimap reset, and the key and locked door restored.
The HUD and minimap sit in the corners without covering the centre of the view, and all HUD text is legible over the dark scene.

title: Recreate a chess endgame still life
prompt:
Recreate the attached render as a three.js scene at 1280x720: a chess endgame still life. A wooden board with a thick dark frame (8 × 8 squares of light maple and darker walnut, with the dark a1 square at the near-left corner) sits on a dark walnut table, seen from White's side, from above and slightly to the right. The pieces are smooth lathe-turned shapes, ivory for White and glossy near-black for Black:
- White: king g1, queen d4, rook e1, pawns f2, g2 and h2.
- Black: king g8, queen c7, rook d8, pawns f7, g7 and h6.
Kings are the tallest pieces and carry a small cross, queens end in a small ball, rooks have a flat hollow top and pawns a round head. To the right of the board a black pawn lies on its side and a white pawn stands on the table, and a polished brass ball rests on the table at the back left. A warm spotlight from the front-left casts soft shadows toward the back-right, a cool rim light comes from behind, and the far end of the table fades into a very dark blue-grey background (fog). Match object positions, sizes, colours, lighting and camera framing as closely as you can, and render a single still frame (no animation is needed).

rubric.criterion: The board matches the target: 8 × 8 alternating light and dark squares with a dark a1 at the near-left, a thick dark frame, and the same size, position and perspective in the frame.
All twelve pieces stand on the right squares with the right types and colours (White Kg1, Qd4, Re1, pawns f2 g2 h2; Black Kg8, Qc7, Rd8, pawns f7 g7 h6).
Piece shapes match: tall kings with crosses, queens with ball tops, flat-topped hollow rooks and round-headed pawns, all smoothly turned.
The extras match: a black pawn lying on its side and a white pawn standing on the table to the right of the board, and a brass ball at the back left.
Materials match: ivory white pieces, glossy near-black pieces with specular highlights, a metallic brass ball, and light maple and darker walnut squares on a dark table.
Lighting matches: a warm key light from the front-left with soft shadows falling toward the back-right, and a darker far side.
The background is a very dark blue-grey and the far part of the table fades into it as in the target.
Camera framing matches: seen from White's side, from a similar height and slightly from the right, with a similar field of view so the board fills the same part of the frame.
The scene is built from three.js meshes and lights rendered to a WebGL canvas, not drawn in 2D or copied from the target image.

title: Recreate a foggy harbor pier at dusk
prompt: Recreate the attached render as a three.js scene at 1280x720: a foggy harbor pier at dusk. The camera stands on a wooden pier, a little above deck height, looking along it as it runs straight away from the viewer into thick purple-grey fog (exponential fog that matches the background colour). The deck is made of planks laid across the pier, with every third plank darker, resting on pairs of round piles above calm, dark blue water; a low rail on posts runs along its left edge. Five black lamp posts stand along the right edge, each topped by a glowing warm-orange lantern whose light makes a pool of light on the planks. A white sailboat with a blue stripe, a single mast and a triangular sail is moored to the left of the pier. Farther back on the left, a red-and-white striped lighthouse with a glowing lamp room and a red cap stands on grey faceted rocks, and faint hill silhouettes line the horizon. A pale full moon hangs in the upper right, and cool moonlight from the back-right casts soft shadows. Match object positions, sizes, colours, lighting, fog density and camera framing as closely as you can, and render a single still frame (no animation is needed).

rubric.criterion: The composition matches: a straight pier receding from the bottom of the frame to a vanishing point at a similar place, seen from a similar height and field of view.
The deck is made of cross planks with every third plank darker, resting on pairs of round piles in the water, with a low rail on posts along the left edge.
Five lamp posts stand along the right edge with glowing warm lanterns that cast pools of warm light on the deck, fading into the fog with distance.
A white sailboat with a blue stripe, one mast and a triangular sail is moored to the left of the pier at a similar size and position.
A red-and-white striped lighthouse with a glowing lamp room and a red cap stands on grey faceted rocks at the back left.
The fog matches: a purple-grey exponential fog equal to the background colour, with objects fading at a similar rate with distance, and faint hill silhouettes on the horizon.
A pale round moon sits in the upper right as in the target.
The palette matches: dusky purple-grey sky, dark blue water, brown planks and warm orange light pools.
The scene is built from three.js meshes and lights rendered to a WebGL canvas, not drawn in 2D or copied from the target image.
